title: A Coach's Dilemma
protagonist: Coach John Cavenaugh, Memphis Tigers head coach
primary_metric: single-attempt make probability, in percentage points: the season free-throw percentage of the Kansas player Memphis chooses to foul, vs. the season three-point percentage of Kansas's most dangerous three-point shooter -- the two live numbers Coach Cavenaugh is actually weighing in the moment

options.A: Commit an intentional foul, sending Kansas to a one-and-one free throw
options.B: Play defense and contest Kansas's final shot

legacy_conversion_note: The original docx (source/Y1/Session 1/A Coach_s Dilemma/Case Study_ A Coach's Dilemma.docx) presents this as real history: a specific '2017-2018 University Of Memphis Tigers' team, a fictional coach 'John Cavenaugh,' and a fictional star player 'Simar Rose' described as being 'drafted #1 in the NBA draft' and becoming 'the youngest player ever to win the NBA Most Valuable Player award.' None of this is real. The real University of Memphis has never won an NCAA championship; no coach named John Cavenaugh or player named Simar Rose exists in its record. The scenario is a fictionalized retelling of the REAL 2008 NCAA Men's Basketball Championship (Kansas defeated Memphis 75-68 in overtime, after Memphis missed the front end of a 1-and-1 free throw late and Kansas's Mario Chalmers hit a game-tying 3-pointer) -- confirmed by the legacy Guide Notes.docx itself, which closes with 'End video: Memphis vs Kansas (last 10 seconds)', a clear reference to the real 2008 finish. This conversion keeps the case AS FICTION (a hypothetical end-game coaching decision), not as a claim about real history: case.md's Overview/Background strip the checkable-false claims (the specific year, 'a feat never before achieved in the history of the school's basketball program', the youngest-MVP claim attached to a fictional player) and state plainly that the scenario is invented, loosely inspired by a real, famous finish. The player box-score and season-stat numbers in Appendix B/C are the original legacy authors' own invented, internally self-consistent dataset (verified byte-identical between the docx tables and the accompanying Championship Game Statistics.xlsx / Season Statistics.xlsx workbooks) -- kept as-is as the case's given fictional dataset, the same way a word-problem's numbers don't need an external citation. What WAS externally verified via WebSearch and is real, current, and cited in sources[]: (1) the NCAA men's basketball one-and-one bonus rule itself (awarded on a team's 7th foul of a half; still in effect for the 2025-26 season, unlike the NCAA women's and NFHS high-school games which have both since replaced it with a two-shot bonus), and (2) the rule that a missed front-end free throw is a LIVE ball reboundable by either team -- this second fact is the case's authored Twist (see FACILITATOR.md), since the legacy source had no twist of its own, only a follow-up discussion question ('what variables have we not accounted for'). A third unused legacy file (Offensive And Defensive Ratings And Rankings.xlsx) was reviewed and excluded -- it is not referenced anywhere in the docx's Background or Challenges, and including it would create an orphan appendix.

modeling_assumptions.text: This case is fiction, not a claim about a real game: the coach, players, final score, and season are all invented by the original case authors (see legacy_conversion_note). Only the one-and-one free-throw rule mechanics (Appendix D, sourced S1-S3) are claims about the real world.

Each Kansas player's season shooting percentage (Appendix C) is used as the modeled probability that player makes any single attempt of that type (free throw, 2-point, or 3-point) in the final possession -- a real, stated simplification. It does not account for defensive pressure specific to a game-ending possession, fatigue, or the specific defender assigned, all of which real coaches also weigh.

The two free throws in a one-and-one are modeled as identical, independent-probability attempts at the shooter's season free-throw percentage p: the shooter must make the first attempt to earn the second, so P(both made) = p^2 (Appendix D, Statistics And Probability: Independent Event).

Kansas trails 62-60 with under 4 seconds left and the ball; a made 2-point shot ties the game (sending it to overtime), and a made 3-point shot wins it outright. This case does not model or require computing what happens in a hypothetical overtime period.

deliverables.text: A season shooting-percentage table (free-throw %, 2-point %, 3-point %) for each of the 8 Kansas players who played in the championship game, computed from their season makes and attempts (Appendix C).
An identification of Kansas's best and worst season free-throw shooter, and best and worst season three-point shooter, among the 8 who played -- with the percentage that makes each one the pick.
The one-and-one probability: the chance the fouled player converts both free throws (sending the game to overtime), computed from that player's own season free-throw percentage.

A side-by-side comparison of the single-shot percentages Coach Cavenaugh is really weighing (the fouled player's free-throw percentage vs. Kansas's most dangerous three-point shooter's percentage) against the true compound one-and-one probability from D3 -- with a written explanation of why the two comparisons point in different directions.
An original bar graph comparing free-throw, 2-point, and 3-point percentages for at least 4 of the 8 Kansas players who played in the championship game.

balance.argument_a: Fouling Diego Imor -- Kansas's worst season free-throw shooter among the 8 who played, at 54.1% -- is the higher-percentage play once the math is done correctly. A one-and-one requires TWO makes, not one: Imor has to make the front end just to earn the second attempt, so his real chance of tying the game is 54.1% squared, a lower 29.3% -- well below Charmers' 46.8% chance of winning it outright on a single contested three. The intentional foul is also the safer strategy on its own terms: it caps Kansas's best case at a tie (overtime), so Memphis is guaranteed at least a fair shot to win later, while a made three on defense ends the game immediately with zero recourse. Both the probability and the downside favor the foul.
balance.argument_b: The single-shot comparison Coach Cavenaugh actually sees in the huddle -- Imor's 54.1% free-throw percentage vs. Charmers' 46.8% three-point percentage -- genuinely favors defense: a defended, contested shot at 46.8% is less likely to go in than a free, uncontested one at 54.1%. Fouling also guarantees Kansas gets to the line at all (no chance of a stop, a deflection, a bad pass, a shot-clock/game-clock violation, or a missed catch under pressure that ends the possession with zero Memphis risk) and carries its own real downside: a foul call anywhere on the floor, an over-the-back or reach-in that officials could rule differently than intended, or a continuation call if Kansas is already in a shooting motion. Playing defense makes Kansas beat Memphis with a shot, rather than handing them two guaranteed, undefended attempts.
balance.margin_basis: Single-attempt make probability: Diego Imor's season free-throw percentage (54.1%, Appendix C) is 7.3 percentage points higher than Cooper Charmers' season three-point percentage (46.8%, Appendix C) -- close enough to genuinely debate, and directly one of the case's own required comparisons (D1/D4). The much larger real gap this produces once the free-throw route is correctly modeled as a compound (squared) probability -- 29.3% vs. 46.8%, a 17.5-point, ~60% relative gap -- is real, computed, and disclosed in D3/D4 and FACILITATOR.md, but is not the graded primary metric: it is the case's central 'trap' (see below), not a close call SPEC's 20% balance cap could honestly cover once revealed. See derived{} for the full worked figures.
balance.stability: NOT stable under a ±50% flex of either compared season percentage (see sensitivity_model.py, probe 5). Flexing fouled_player_ft_pct (Diego Imor's season free-throw %, 54.1%) to -50% (27.05%) FLIPS the winner to Option B, margin 73.0%; to +50% (81.15%) Option A still wins but by 73.4%, breaking the SPEC §2 20% cap either way. Flexing defended_shooter_3pt_pct (Cooper Charmers' season three-point %, 46.8%) to +50% (70.185%) FLIPS the winner to Option B, margin 29.7%, breaking the cap; to -50% (23.395%) Option A still wins but by 131.2%, also breaking the cap. twist_rebound_risk does not affect this comparison (it only affects the Twist's separate compound accounting) and is stable at ±50% by construction. No honest retune of a stated constraint closes this: both flexed values are the case's own real, internally-consistent Appendix C season stats, verified byte-identical to the original legacy workbooks (see legacy_conversion_note) -- there is no other numeric assumption dial behind this comparison to adjust without fabricating data. Per DOCTRINE_LEDGER.md MCS-26/MCS-41, disclosure is the required response, not elimination: probe 5 is a permanent, disclosed mechanical FAIL for this case, not a pass earned by disclosure -- see FACILITATOR.md's Sensitivity note and Lessons Learned.
